prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item also shows your previous context and question. Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

Kind of decision: whether to continue or drop a line of work
Problem: Whether current alignment tools (interpretability, training-based methods, control) are adequate.
Write-up text before the decision: .com/posts/FJJ9ff73adnantXiA/alignment-will-happen-by-default-what-s-next?commentId=bWjmGAuEBZKTr6Aay HIS COMMENT: I'm very surprised that people seem to update this way. [...] There were a lot of things that caught developers by surprise, e.g., the reward hacking of the coding models, or emergent misalignment-related issues, or eval awareness messing with the results. My overall sense is also that high-compute agentic RL makes all problems much harder because you reward the model on consequences, and it's hard to set exactly the right constraints in that setting. I also think eval awareness is rapidly rising and makes alignment harder across the board, and makes scheming-related issues plausible for the first time in real models. I also feel like none of the tools we have right now really work very well. They are all reducing the problem a bit, potentially enough to carry us for a while, but not enough that I would deeply trust a system built by them. \- Interpretability is somewhat useful now, but still not quite able to be used for effective debugging or aligning the internal concepts of the model. \- Training-based methods seem to work in a reductionist way, e.g., our anti-scheming training generalized better than I anticipated, but it is clearly not enough, and I don't know how to close the gap. \- Control seems promising, but still needs to be validated in practice in much more detail.
Previous context: A research team reviewing the past year of evidence finds interpretability somewhat useful but not yet adequate for debugging or aligning internal concepts, training-based methods that reduce but do not close the gap (though anti-scheming training generalized better than expected), and control approaches that are promising but unvalidated in practice. None of the current tools work well enough for the team to deeply trust a system built with them. The team must decide how to weigh continued investment across these directions.
Previous question: Given that current tools only partially reduce the problem, how should the team prioritize continued work across interpretability, training-based methods, and control?
